summary:
Arizona sits within the United States federal framework, and that framework governs the documents a trans visitor carries. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Checkpoint screening adds exposure at Phoenix Sky Harbor and Tucson International: Transportation Security Administration procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller, and from February 2025 the State Department treats a visa applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud with a permanent bar.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Arizona in its low-risk group alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, describing these jurisdictions as having largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. Arizona is named alongside Virginia as having enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies that the assessment judges unlikely to be extended to adults. The assessment is a July 2026 judgement, not a guarantee, and several of the federal measures it sits under remain blocked or enjoined in court.

State identity documents are more accessible than the federal position suggests. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a signed physician statement attesting that the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery. Birth certificate change without sex reassignment surgery was permitted by a federal judge's order of August 2024 in litigation brought in November 2020 by three families with transgender children against the Arizona Department of Health Services, joined by all resident transgender individuals, with the case ongoing as of August 2023.

Employment and public-accommodation protection exists at three levels. The 2020 rulings in Bostock v. Clayton County, Altitude Express v. Zarda and Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC protect gender-identity discrimination in employment under Title VII. A January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banned gender-identity discrimination in state employment and contracts, and a June 2023 Attorney General affirmation held that state sex discrimination includes gender identity. Municipal ordinances in Phoenix (revised February 2013), Flagstaff (March 2013), Tempe (February 2014), Sedona (2015), Winslow (November 2018), Mesa (March 2021), Scottsdale (April 2021, effective 20 May), Glendale (May 2021) and Tolleson (June 2021) ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses.

Criminal-law protection is uneven. Arizona hate-crime law does not include gender identity, while the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act has covered gender identity since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under common law, and reform bills have lapsed without action.

Facilities and sport rules in Arizona target minors rather than adults. In March 2023 the Governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and vetoed an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools. A second March 2022 bill signed by Governor Doug Ducey legally bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition, effective 30 days after enactment. No Arizona statute barring trans adults from facilities is sourced here.

Medical access has contradictory layers. A 1982 regulation provides that Medicaid cannot cover sex reassignment surgery, challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with the National Center for Lesbian Rights, the National Health Law Program and co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits seeking to void the ban. A June 2023 executive order granted Arizona government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. In March 2022 the Legislature passed and Governor Ducey signed a ban on sex reassignment surgery on transgender children, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children, effective March 2023.

Conversion therapy was banned by Pima County in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines of up to 2,500 dollars, and a June 2023 executive order banned government funding for conversion therapy. Arizona Supreme Court authority of 25 April 2019 allows family courts to determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances where divorced parents reach impasse, deciding disputed parenting-plan elements and other factors necessary for emotional and physical health, narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm.
tangentialFactors:
Arizona's political environment is affecting queer civic life even where the law does not. Tucson Pride cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Prism reported the decision on 3 June 2026 and grouped Tucson with Tampa, Florida and Arlington, Texas as affected cities.

Arizona is grouped by the July 2026 risk assessment with states judged to have refrained from targeting transgender adults, while the same assessment treats state-level document invalidation elsewhere as a template. Kansas enacted a law in March 2026 invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth, which rights groups describe as a model for other state legislatures; Arizona's physician-statement route for licence amendment stands in the opposite direction, and the direction of travel in neighbouring legislatures is not settled.

Indigenous traditions in the region predate Western categories of gender. Navajo recognition includes four roles, among them nádleehi, defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature whose identity is fluid, perceived as balanced between sexes and typically chosen for communal roles such as spiritual healers, traditionally wearing female clothes and doing female work, with some having sexual relations with men accepted by the tribe. Parallel terms include wi:k'ovat among Tohono O'odham, hova among Hopi, alyha and hwame among Mohave, and ilyaxai' and kwiraxame' among Maricopa, part of what is now increasingly called two-spirit identity. Will Roscoe's work records that the prevalence of such conduct and the tolerance or even respect shown to transgender people fuelled Spanish explorers' arguments for colonisation, and Jonathan Ned Katz describes Christianisation as including attempts to eliminate traditional Indigenous homosexuality as cultural genocide. Will Roscoe's work and Katz's analysis are cited here as historical evidence of how colonial authorities treated gender variance.

Public opinion in Arizona is measured as broadly supportive of non-discrimination protection: 2019 Public Religion Research Institute polling found 71% of Arizona residents supported LGBTQ non-discrimination legislation, while 2017 PRRI findings recorded 63% support for same-sex marriage, 73% support for anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 59% opposition to religious refusals to serve LGBTQ people.

Reported outcomes among Indigenous residents are severe: 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempt suicide, and LGBT Navajo may find it difficult to be accepted by family.
localsOnly:
State employment and contracting are covered by the January 2023 executive order banning gender-identity discrimination, reinforced by the June 2023 Attorney General affirmation, and by the 2020 Title VII rulings. Sexual-orientation protections run in parallel through a 1992 Phoenix ordinance for city and contract workers, a 1999 Tucson ordinance, a 2003 Governor Napolitano order for state employees, and the 2013-2021 municipal ordinances. A June 2023 executive order granted Arizona government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised since a United States district court decision of 17 October 2014 forced an end to enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, which remain textually in the state constitution and Arizona Revised Statutes and on the Legislature website as unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and, for out-of-state recognition, the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act. Voters rejected Proposition 107 in November 2006 and approved Proposition 102 in November 2008, after which cities including Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff enacted domestic partnerships or civil unions.

Adoption is permitted with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, though primary consideration goes to married couples unless a married couple is unavailable or contrary to the child's best interest. Lesbian couples have IVF access, state law recognises a non-genetic, non-gestational married mother via donor insemination, and the Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights under Obergefell v. Hodges and Pavan v. Smith to list both names on birth certificates, implemented by an October 2020 Appeals order. Surrogacy, gestational or traditional, is prohibited and contracts unenforceable, though Soos v. Superior Court (1994) allows pre-birth orders for biological parents and requires second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent. An April 2022 emergency law signed by Governor Ducey allows religious organizations to discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

Schools carry reporting machinery. In March 2023 the Department of Education introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In April 2019 the Legislature repealed a 1991 law prohibiting AIDS or HIV instruction that portrayed safe methods of homosexual sex positively, by House 55-5 and Senate 19-10, effective 1 July 2019 amid court challenges. Governor Ducey vetoed SB1456 on 20 April 2021, which had required parental opt-in for sex, gender identity and sexuality teaching after 31-28 House and 16-14 Senate passage, and a watered-down successor advanced in June 2021. Governor Brewer vetoed a February 2014 religious-freedom bill widely reported as targeting LGBTQ people.

Hate-crime law in Arizona includes sexual orientation as a protected category providing additional penalties for bias-motivated crimes, but not gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity is legal following the Arizona Equity Act of 2001, which repealed sodomy laws that had carried penalties of five to twenty years plus sheriff registration requirements under the 1951 code. Phoenix and Tucson host prominent LGBTQ communities, Tucson Pride having been founded in 1977 as the first in the state and the first Phoenix Pride parade held in 1981.

The July 2026 assessment's judgement that Arizona's youth-targeting policies are unlikely to be extended to adults is an assessment, not a legal finding; whether any Arizona legislature will move adult facility, document or care restrictions is unresolved and not sourced.

The August 2024 federal order permitting birth certificate change without surgery resolves the claim as stated, but the inventory does not establish whether the November 2020 litigation has been finally terminated or whether appellate challenge remains open.

Arizona hate-crime law's omission of gender identity is stated as current; the status of reform bills that lapsed without action, and whether any successor is pending, is unresolved.

The 1982 Medicaid bar on sex reassignment surgery is described as challenged since 2019 and 2020; whether it remains operative alongside the June 2023 executive order covering state employees over 21 is unresolved in this inventory.

Several federal measures bearing on documents, facilities and care, including the passport sex-marker restriction, have been blocked or enjoined in court at various points, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
